NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
This intervention proposes a closed-loop acid concentration setpoint reduction and inhibitor dosing procedure change to suppress hydrogen pickup. Standard practice maintains a fixed, high acid concentration (15%) and static inhibitor level to ensure scale removal speed, which maximizes the hydrogen overpotential driving force at the strip surface. This mitigation departs by dynamically lowering the acid concentration setpoint to the minimum threshold required for effective scale attack, while simultaneously increasing the inhibitor dosing rate to a specific conductance-derived target, thereby shifting the electrochemical equilibrium to suppress the reduction reaction that generates atomic hydrogen. The adjacent-technique clearance is that this is not standard "inhibitor addition" (which is a static bulk treatment) but a "concentration-inhibitor coupling" where the inhibitor dose is parameterized by real-time conductivity (surrogate for acid strength) to maintain a critical inhibitor-to-acid ratio, and the departure element is the interconnection of the concentration setpoint with the dosing algorithm.

PHYSICS CHECK
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = hydrogen overpotential (or hydrogen flux) at the steel surface; the mechanism moves it DOWN by reducing the acid activity (lowering $a_{H^+}$) and increasing the inhibitor coverage factor ($\theta$), which lowers the anodic rate of steel dissolution and critically reduces the cathodic hydrogen evolution rate; this REDUCES the hydrogen embrittlement damage integral over the duty cycle.
The governing relation is the Butler-Volmer equation for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), where the rate is proportional to $a_{H^+}^{\beta}$ and inversely related to the inhibitor blocking factor. Lowering acid concentration from 15% (approx. 5 M) to the minimum effective level (e.g., 8-10%, approx. 3-4 M) reduces the hydrogen diffusion flux $J_H \propto \frac{D_H \Delta C_H}{L}$. By reducing the source concentration $\Delta C_H$ of hydrogen at the interface, the bulk hydrogen uptake is reduced. Magnitude verification: A 30-40% reduction in acid molarity reduces the theoretical hydrogen generation rate by a similar order of magnitude (approx. 30-40%), provided scale removal remains kinetic-controlled by temperature/tension rather than mass-limited by acid depletion.

MECHANISM CLASS: Chemistry/Setpoint Coupling

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
MECHANISM CLASS: Chemistry/Setpoint Coupling
*   (c) Acid Concentration Setpoint: Lower the HCl acid concentration control setpoint from 15% to 10% (or the minimum supplier-recommended level for scale removal at 70 C) using the existing acid dosing valve control loop. This is a parameter change to the existing variable frequency drive (VFD) or valve positioner that already modulates acid dosing.
*   (c) Inhibitor Dosing Procedure: Modify the inhibitor dosing controller logic to increase the base dosing rate by 20-30% relative to the standard recipe, and implement a conductivity-compensated boost: when bath conductivity (proxy for acid strength) dips below a threshold (indicating over-dilution or low acid), the inhibitor dose is maintained at the higher base rate to ensure the inhibitor-to-acid ratio does not fall below the critical threshold for fluting prevention. This uses the existing conductivity transmitter and dosing pump already installed in the line.
*   (c) Line Speed Schedule: No change to line speed is required if the reduced acid concentration maintains sufficient scale removal rate; however, if scale removal lags, a minor speed reduction (5%) may be scheduled during start-up transients only, executed via the existing line speed controller. Operational loss: 0 for steady state, negligible for start-up.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
*   (c) Acid Setpoint Change: Zero new hardware. The existing acid dosing valve and controller are used as-is. Burden is zero.
*   (c) Inhibitor Dosing Procedure Change: Zero new hardware. The existing inhibitor dosing pump and conductivity transmitter are used as-is. The burden is purely procedural (updating the PLC recipe or PID setpoints). Operational loss: 0. The cost of inhibitor is slightly increased (20-30%), which is offset by the reduced rate of strip rejections/fluting and potential reduction in acid consumption due to lower concentration.
*   (c) Line Speed Schedule: Zero new hardware. Burden is zero. Operational loss: 0 in steady state.
Conclusion: The intervention adds no hardware, no custom parts, and no process development. It is a pure parameter and procedure change on existing infrastructure, concluding same-or-lower burden class (specifically, lower installation burden than standard practice which maintains fixed setpoints).
EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Conduct a 48-hour run on the pickling line at the new setpoints (10% HCl, increased inhibitor dose). Measure strip surface quality (visual inspection for fluting) and hydrogen content (stainless steel trap method or optical spectroscopy if available) on sample coupons taken from the line. Pass/Fail Thresholds: No new fluting defects observed compared to baseline; hydrogen content reduced by >20% relative to standard practice. Duration: 48 hours (covers 3-4 shifts). Kill Criterion: If scale removal rate drops by >15% (measured by thickness profile), revert to 15% acid and maintain higher inhibitor dose; if fluting persists despite inhibitor boost, the mechanism is failed.
